transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 90 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Ferri (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (OptiRetail - Head of ML), Tom Nguyen (OptiRetail - Platform Eng), Priya Rao (OptiRetail - SRE)
Recorded at: 2026-07-22T15:00:00-07:00

Summary (auto): technical deep dive focusing on differences between Redwood Dedicated and Hosted, runtime performance (latency/throughput), KV cache behaviour, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Customer is concerned about noisy neighbor isolation and throughput guarantees for peak traffic (Black Friday-like spikes).

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we wanted to leave 90 minutes for this, Luca will drive the runtime and perf bits, I'll jump in on platform and procurement questions. Sara, Tom, Priya, nice to meet you.
[00:12] Sara: Hey Maya, hi Luca. Quick context: we're OptiRetail, heavy peak season traffic, doing personalized recommender + conversational search. We evaluated some open models and also have a small self-host experiment. Main ask: can we get guaranteed throughput and predictable latency for spikes without paying huge unit costs?
[00:28] Luca: Great. I'll start high level then dig into KV cache and batching. Very roughly: Hosted is fastest to get going, dynamic multi-tenant clusters, cost-efficient for variable load. Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity, isolation, predictable throughput, and stronger SLOs for p95/p99.
[00:45] Tom: When you say isolation, do you mean hardware isolation or network only? Concern is noisy neighbor — we've seen noisy neighbor on other cloud providers where shared HW plus other customers running big batches kill our p95.
[00:58] Luca: Good question. Dedicated means a pool of GPUs reserved for your tenancy: hardware isolation in the sense that you don't share the same GPU instances with other tenants. There are also VM-level limits and cgroup tuning for noisy neighbor mitigation. In Hosted, we use request shaping and routing tiers, but it's still multi-tenant so you can get variability.
[01:18] Priya: How do you guarantee throughput? If we commit to X tokens/sec, is that a contract? We need to know how autoscaling behaves under sudden bursts.
[01:26] Maya: For Dedicated we offer reserved capacity contracts — you get a committed number of GPUs and SLAs for throughput/latency. Autoscaling policies can be configured (burst capacity, warm pools). For Hosted we have best-effort SLOs and throttles.
[01:38] Luca: I want to show the important runtime levers: 1) batching: larger batches improve GPU utilization and tokens/sec but add tail latency. 2) KV cache: prefix caching avoids re-computation for repeated contexts and can reduce token generation work dramatically. 3) quantization: model size/throughput tradeoffs, e.g., q4_0 or int8 can double throughput with small quality delta depending on model.
[01:56] Sara: On KV cache — what's the eviction policy, and where is it stored? We care about memory footprint; if it spills to disk that will kill latency.
[02:05] Luca: KV cache lives in-GPU memory in both Dedicated and Hosted when we pin the model to a worker. For long-tail sessions we do LRU-ish eviction and also segment by conversation id. In Dedicated, you can configure cache sizes per model because you control pool sizing; in Hosted, cache is automatic and evictions may be more aggressive if the cluster is rebalanced. We avoid spilling to disk for production paths — if you see spilling that's indicative of a mis-config or using an oversized context.
[02:30] Tom: Is the KV cache warm on restarts? If we have node replacement during autoscale, do we lose the cache?
[02:36] Luca: If a worker dies the KV cache is lost unless you use our sticky sessions + warm pool. For Dedicated you can enable warm standby nodes that keep model weights and pre-warmed KV slots. For Hosted, we have heuristics for warming but not guaranteed persistence. That is one of the big reasons customers choose Dedicated for latency-sensitive workloads.
[02:58] Sara: What about batching strategy? We can't accept 200ms extra for user-facing chat on mobile.
[03:05] Luca: We tune batching by target latency SLO. For example: target p95 300ms -> keep batchers to small sizes and use dynamic batching with a short max wait (5-10ms). For throughput-heavy backfill jobs you can use large fixed batches. In Dedicated you can size pool to allow high concurrency and still keep small real-time batch sizes. Hosted can autotune but may multiplex workloads into bigger batches under heavy load, which increases p95 variance.
[03:33] Priya: Any numbers? tokens/sec per GPU for your recommended quantization profiles?
[03:38] Luca: Rough examples (approx, subject to model and sequence length): for a 30B decoder model unquantized you might see ~120-200 tokens/sec on an A100-class GPU; q4_0 can push that to ~220-350 tokens/sec. With QAT/int8 kernels on newer runtimes we see ~2-3x speedups for some models. We'll send exact benchmark sheets for the specific model variants you're considering.
[04:02] Sara: And latency per token? p95 on short completions?
[04:06] Luca: Latency per token depends on batching and KV hit rate. A cache hit for prefix tokens basically removes the decoding cost of earlier tokens, so you can get sub-100ms increments per token on local GPU for short prompts with small batches. But tail p99 matters: if a big batch happens it'll push p99 higher. That's why Dedicated plus warm pools gives the most predictable tails.
[04:28] Tom: We have VPC-only requirement for PCI/PPI regulated flows. How does Redwood Private work with KV cache and warm pools — any networking gotchas?
[04:37] Maya: Redwood Private deploys the control plane outside your VPC and the data plane can run inside your VPC or on-prem. For KV cache and warm pools the data plane nodes are in your network so cold-starts are within your environment. You can also enable customer-managed KMS/HSM for key management. Networking things we see: egress rules, NAT gateways, and cross-AZ bandwidth for large model shards — those need planning.
[04:58] Priya: Can we air-gap for some of our infra? We have one environment that is fully isolated.
[05:02] Maya: We do an on-prem package; air-gapped installs are possible but require an enterprise engagement. They include offline package delivery and a private control plane option.
[05:12] Sara: What about model variants and fallbacks? If the Dedicated pool saturates, do you have automatic fallbacks to a cheaper hosted variant?
[05:19] Luca: Yes — smart routing can route to a compatible hosted model on overflow, or route to a smaller quantized variant. You can configure automatic fallback policies per route, with cost/latency thresholds. In Dedicated you can also set a burst capacity that uses shared spare capacity for short bursts.
[05:37] Tom: Noisy neighbor again: suppose another tenant (on hosted) blasts the cluster and we get degraded perf — can you set priority QoS?
[05:45] Luca: In Hosted we use priority routing and rate limiting but it's fundamentally multi-tenant. For hard QoS and isolation you want Dedicated, where only your workloads run on that pool. We also recommend isolation at the network level (VPC, subnets) and RBAC to limit noisy job types.
[06:00] Sara: On quantization: do you support mixed precision kernels and fallback to float16 for quality critical prompts? We need to preserve recommendation accuracy for sensitive queries.
[06:09] Luca: Yes — our runtime supports multiple kernels; you can specify quant profiles per route. Mixed-precision is common: run most requests with q4_0 for throughput, and route a small percentage (or specific prompt types) to fp16 for quality checks. We also support A/B testing and eval hooks to detect quality regressions.
[06:28] Priya: Any security concerns with caching user PII in KV cache?
[06:33] Maya: Good point. KV cache can contain user-specific context. For regulated data you can configure encryption at rest and strict retention policies or disable persistent caching. For Dedicated/Private you can point logs and traces to your internal collectors and limit retention.
[06:49] Sara: How do you do autoscaling deterministically? We need to know how quickly the system can add nodes to handle spikes and what the cold-start penalty is.
[06:58] Luca: Autoscaling is policy-driven. For Dedicated we recommend a warm pool sized for expected bursts (e.g., x% of baseline). Scale-up is fast if warm nodes are present (seconds), otherwise cold starts involve model load time (could be 1-3 minutes for very large models). Hosted has more pooled capacity so cold-starts are generally faster but not guaranteed.
[07:20] Tom: For the pilot we want to measure p95 and throughput under a synthetic peak test that mirrors Black Friday patterns — can you provide a benchmark harness?
[07:26] Maya: Yes, we'll provide the benchmark harness and a spreadsheet with expected tokens/sec, memory footprints, and recommended batch/quant profiles. We'll also include a sample traffic pattern file you can replay.
[07:36] Sara: Pricing question — with Dedicated we pay for reserved GPUs even if they're idle; is there a hybrid option to offload overflow to Hosted and only pay Hosted runtime when used?
[07:45] Maya: Yes, hybrid routing is a common pattern: reserved Dedicated baseline + overflow to Hosted. Costs are predictable for baseline and variable for overflow. We can model cost scenarios for you in the sheet.
[07:55] Luca: A few operational notes: 1) measure real sequence length distribution — most perf tuning hinges on that, 2) instrument KV hit rate and batching stats per route, 3) use warm pools for strict latency SLOs.
[08:12] Priya: Are there known model architectures that don't play well with your quant kernels? We've tried some community models that break when q4_0 is applied.
[08:19] Luca: Some older decoder-only variants or exotic ops can have limited optimized kernels; our model onboarding team can validate and provide recommended quant profiles. For those we sometimes recommend running a fp16 serving profile. We'll include a compatibility matrix.
[08:31] Sara: Ok let's recap the open questions and next steps.
[08:35] Maya: Recap: 1) Redwood Dedicated gives hardware isolation and predictable tails; Hosted is faster to start and cheaper for variable workloads. 2) KV cache in-GPU reduces compute but needs warm pools to avoid cold cache penalties. 3) Batching tradeoffs mean you should size pools for expected concurrency if you need low p95. 4) Quantization can improve throughput 2x-3x but test for quality regressions; use mixed profiles and eval hooks. 5) For VPC/on-prem we can do Private or on-prem air-gapped with extra enterprise support.
[08:58] Tom: Action items — we'll send our p95 SLOs and traffic pattern.
[09:02] Maya: Great. We'll send the benchmark sheet, SOC2/network docs, and propose pilot dates.
[09:08] Sara: Thanks everyone, that was great.
[09:10] Luca: Thanks — will follow up with configs and numbers.
[09:12] End of recording.

References mentioned: benchmark spreadsheet (link: /redwood/benchmarks/optiretail-2026-07.xlsx), SOC2 & network architecture doc (link: /redwood/security/soc2_and_network.pdf), pilot proposal deck (link noted in chat).
